title: Episode 129: Zachary Taylor and the White House: Old Rough and Ready
description:
Zachary Taylor was perhaps the most improbable man ever elected President of the United States. A career frontier soldier who had spent forty years in backwoods forts from Indiana to Florida, Taylor had never held political office, had never voted in a presidential election in his entire life, and had no formal political ideology. He hated military pomp, dressed in a wrinkled straw hat and a stained civilian duster, chewed tobacco incessantly, and rode his favorite warhorse Old Whitey with one leg hooked casually over the saddle horn, earning the affectionate nickname 'Old Rough and Ready.'

Following his miraculous victory over Santa Anna at the Battle of Buena Vista in eighteen forty-seven, the Whig Party desperately drafted Taylor as their presidential candidate. Taylor was so indifferent to politics that he almost missed his official nomination: because the Whig National Convention mailed the letter with unpaid postage, Taylor refused to pay the ten cents in delivery fees and left the letter sitting in the dead-letter office for weeks!

Yet once in the White House, this Louisiana slaveholder shocked the nation. When Southern radicals threatened secession over the admission of California as a free state, Old Rough and Ready drew a line of iron. Chewing tobacco in the Oval Office, Taylor warned Southern leaders that if they raised a finger of rebellion against the Union, he would personally take the field as Commander-in-Chief and hang anyone caught in armed rebellion with less remorse than he had hanged spies in Mexico. Here is George with the extraordinary story of America's rugged soldier-president.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we step into the presidency of our twelfth chief executive, Zachary Taylor. Taylor was a rough-hewn soldier who spent forty years sleeping in frontier tents, fighting in swamps, and chewing tobacco. He had never voted, had no political party, and never wanted the presidency. Yet when the nation plunged into a crisis that threatened civil war in eighteen forty-nine, this unpolished general showed a fierce, uncompromising devotion to the American Union. Here is George with the story of Old Rough and Ready.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: FORTY YEARS ON THE FRONTIER
Zachary Taylor was a child of the wilderness. Born in Virginia in seventeen eighty-four into a prominent planter family, he was carried as an infant across the Appalachian Mountains in a wicker basket to the raw frontier of Kentucky near Louisville. Growing up in a log cabin surrounded by dense forests and hostile Native tribes, young Zachary received virtually no formal schooling. He learned to track game, swim freezing rivers, and handle a flintlock musket with deadly accuracy.
In eighteen-eight, President Thomas Jefferson granted twenty-three-year-old Taylor a commission as a first lieutenant in the United States Army. It was the beginning of a forty-year military career that saw Taylor stationed in virtually every remote, mosquito-infested outpost on the American frontier. During the War of eighteen-twelve, Captain Taylor achieved national fame by successfully defending Fort Harrison in the Indiana Territory against an overwhelming force of Shawnee warriors, earning a brevet promotion to major from James Madison.
For the next three decades, Taylor commanded forts in Wisconsin, Minnesota, Louisiana, and Florida. In the brutal Second Seminole War, Taylor led federal troops into the tangled, snake-infested waters of the Everglades, defeating Seminole warriors at the Battle of Lake Okeechobee on Christmas Day eighteen thirty-seven. Through it all, Taylor never developed a taste for military ceremony, shiny buttons, or formal regulations. He was a practical, mud-splattered soldier who cared for his men, ate the same hardtack rations as private soldiers, and won the unshakeable devotion of the frontier.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE LEGEND OF OLD ROUGH AND READY
By the time the Mexican-American War erupted in eighteen forty-six, sixty-one-year-old Brigadier General Zachary Taylor was an unforgettable, legendary character. Short, stocky, with bowed legs from decades in the saddle, weather-beaten skin that resembled old leather, and unruly gray hair, Taylor looked far more like an impoverished dirt farmer than a commanding general.
Taylor refused to wear a standard army uniform. Instead, he lounged around his headquarters wearing a battered, floppy straw hat, a rumpled brown linen coat, and unbuttoned civilian trousers tucked into mud-caked boots. He chewed tobacco continuously, spitting amber streams of tobacco juice with pinpoint accuracy while dictating battle orders to his staff. His favorite mount was 'Old Whitey'—a calm, battle-scarred white stallion who grazed peacefully around camp and was completely unbothered by cannon fire. Taylor had an eccentric habit of riding Old Whitey with both legs hooked over the same side of the saddle, conversing casually with private soldiers as they marched through the dust.
The soldiers idolized him, baptizing him with the nickname 'Old Rough and Ready.' When volunteer regiments arrived in Texas from across the country, men walked right past Taylor, mistaking him for a local teamster or stable hand. Yet beneath his disheveled exterior lay a man of profound personal courage and tactical calm. Under fire, Taylor was immovable. During the desperate second day of the Battle of Buena Vista, when Mexican cannonballs tore through the dirt around Old Whitey, Taylor calmly patted his horse's neck, adjusted his straw hat, and refused to take cover, inspiring his outnumbered men to fight to the last cartridge.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: THE RELUCTANT CANDIDATE AND THE DEAD-LETTER OFFICE
Following the victory at Buena Vista, a tidal wave of 'Taylor Fever' swept the United States. Americans, weary of hyper-partisan politicians, saw in Old Rough and Ready the second coming of George Washington: a virtuous, unpretentious soldier who put country above party. Whig Party leaders, desperate to win back the presidency in eighteen forty-eight, realized that Taylor was their golden ticket.
There was only one problem: Zachary Taylor had no interest in politics. He had spent his entire life in the army, moving from post to post, and had never cast a ballot in any election in his entire sixty-four years. He had no defined opinions on tariffs, banking, or internal improvements. When reporters asked if he was a Whig or a Democrat, Taylor candidly replied that he was an independent who would be a president of the whole people, adding: 'I am a Whig, but I am not an ultra-Whig.'
The campaign was marked by one of the most hilarious episodes in political history. In the nineteenth century, postage was often paid not by the sender, but by the recipient upon delivery. Because Taylor received hundreds of letters of praise and unsolicited advice from across the country, his post office bill in Baton Rouge was costing him a fortune. Taylor instructed the local postmaster to return all letters with unpaid postage to the dead-letter office.
In June eighteen forty-eight, the Whig National Convention in Philadelphia officially nominated Zachary Taylor for President of the United States and mailed him the formal notification letter—with unpaid postage! The postmaster duly tossed the letter into the dead-letter pile. For weeks, the Whig Party was thrown into frantic panic, wondering why their candidate had not acknowledged his nomination. Only when an anxious Whig envoy traveled to Baton Rouge in person did Taylor learn that he was officially running for President of the United States!

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE ELECTION OF 1848
In the presidential election of eighteen forty-eight, the Whigs ran a brilliant, non-ideological campaign, portraying Taylor as a national unifier. Taylor adopted a simple campaign platform: he promised that if elected, he would respect the independence of Congress, use the presidential veto only in cases of clear constitutional violations, and govern as an impartial magistrate.
The election was a three-way contest. The Democratic Party nominated Lewis Cass of Michigan, who championed the doctrine of 'popular sovereignty'—allowing settlers in new territories to decide for themselves whether to allow slavery. Meanwhile, anti-slavery Northern Democrats and Whigs formed the Free Soil Party, nominating former President Martin Van Buren on the platform of 'Free Soil, Free Speech, Free Labor, and Free Men.'
The Free Soil ticket fractured the Democratic vote in the critical swing state of New York, allowing Taylor to carry the state's thirty-six electoral votes. Taylor swept the South, where voters trusted him as a Louisiana cotton planter who owned over one hundred enslaved people, while also winning key Northern states like Pennsylvania, Massachusetts, and New York. On November seventh, eighteen forty-eight—the first time all states voted on the exact same day—Zachary Taylor was elected the twelfth President of the United States, winning one hundred and sixty-three electoral votes to Cass's one hundred and twenty-seven.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SOUTHERN MISCALCULATION
Southern politicians celebrated Taylor's victory as a magnificent triumph for the slaveholding South. John C. Calhoun and Southern congressmen assumed that because Taylor owned large cotton plantations in Louisiana and Mississippi, he would staunchly defend the expansion of slavery into the vast territories newly won from Mexico. They could not have been more catastrophically wrong.
Zachary Taylor was a Southern planter, but he was first, last, and always a soldier of the United States. He had carried the American flag for forty years in uniform, and his ultimate, non-negotiable loyalty belonged to the perpetuity of the American Union. Furthermore, as a practical Western soldier, Taylor recognized that the arid, mountainous lands of California and New Mexico were geographically unsuited to plantation cotton slavery anyway.
Taylor devised a bold, direct solution to defuse the brewing crisis over slavery expansion. Bypassing the long, contentious territorial stage, Taylor dispatched military agents to California and New Mexico, urging the settlers to immediately draft state constitutions and apply directly for admission to the Union as full states. California, flooded by thousands of Gold Rush miners, drafted a constitution that unanimously banned slavery within its borders and applied for statehood in late eighteen forty-nine. New Mexico prepared to do the same. Southern leaders were stunned into disbelief: a Southern slaveholder in the White House was actively paving the way for two massive free states that would permanently destroy the South's balance of power in the United States Senate.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE STANDOFF IN THE EXECUTIVE MANSION
In early eighteen fifty, Washington detonated into fury. Southern politicians felt betrayed. Mississippi called for a convention of Southern states to meet in Nashville to consider secession, and Texas threatened to send militia to seize eastern New Mexico by force of arms. In Congress, Southern radicals openly threatened disunion if California was admitted as a free state without massive concessions to the South.
In February eighteen fifty, a delegation of furious Southern congressmen, led by Robert Toombs and Alexander Stephens of Georgia, marched into the White House to confront the President. They warned Taylor that if he persisted in supporting California statehood without protecting Southern rights, the South would secede from the Union, and Southern officers in the United States Army would resign to fight for their home states.
Zachary Taylor rose to his feet, his weathered face darkening with terrifying military fury. Old Rough and Ready looked the Southern firebrands in the eye and delivered an ultimatum that chilled them to the bone. Taylor told them that if there was any attempt to disrupt the laws of the United States or seize New Mexico by force, he would not hesitate for a single second: he would personally take command of the United States Army, march into the South at the head of federal troops, put down the rebellion by force of arms, and hang every man taken in rebellion with less reluctance than he had hanged Mexican deserters at Monterrey. The Southern congressmen left the White House in stunned, shaken silence. The old general meant every word.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE GRANITE PATRIOT
While Henry Clay and Daniel Webster worked in the Senate to craft an elaborate compromise package—what would eventually become the Compromise of eighteen fifty—Zachary Taylor stood like an unyielding granite block. Taylor opposed Clay's omnibus compromise, insisting that California had an inherent constitutional right to immediate, unconditional statehood as a free state, without making concessions to Southern threats of disunion.
Taylor's presidency demonstrated that true patriotism transcends regional origin and economic self-interest. Though born in the South, enriched by Southern cotton, and surrounded by Southern advisers, Taylor refused to allow sectional radicals to hold the American republic hostage. He brought to the presidency the plain, direct virtues of the American frontier: honesty, simplicity, and unbending courage.
Yet just as the titanic political showdown reached its absolute climax, fate struck a cruel, shocking blow. The rugged old general, who had survived forty years of Indian wars, yellow fever, dysentery, and Mexican cannonballs, was about to be felled not by an assassin's bullet or a battlefield foe, but by an ordinary, festive celebration on America's birthday.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Zachary Taylor proved that an unpolished frontier soldier could stand as a giant of constitutional patriotism, refusing to bow to threats of disunion. Next week, we explore the shocking, sudden tragedy that ended his presidency: the Fourth of July celebration in eighteen fifty, the deadly bowl of cherries and iced milk, and the century-long mystery over whether Old Rough and Ready was secretly assassinated by poison. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
